related_questions.question: What to do after being diagnosed with diabetes?

text_blocks.snippet: After a diabetes diagnosis, focus on creating a management plan with your healthcare team, adopting healthy lifestyle habits, and seeking support. This involves understanding your blood glucose targets, learning how to monitor your levels, and making dietary and exercise adjustments.
snippet_highlighted_words: focus on creating a management plan with your healthcare team, adopting healthy lifestyle habits, and seeking support

list.snippet: Primary care physician: Your doctor will be your main point of contact for diabetes management.
Endocrinologist: A specialist in hormone disorders, they can provide additional expertise in managing diabetes, especially for Type 1.
Certified diabetes care and education specialist (CDCES): These professionals provide education and support on managing diabetes.
Other healthcare professionals: Consider consulting with a registered dietitian, a certified diabetes educator, or a mental health professional, as needed.

text_blocks.snippet: 2. Understand Your Diabetes and Develop a Plan:

list.title: Learn about diabetes:
list.snippet: Educate yourself on the different types of diabetes, its causes, symptoms, and potential complications.

list.title: Create a personalized treatment plan:
list.snippet: Work with your healthcare team to establish blood glucose targets, medication schedules (if needed), and strategies for managing blood sugar levels.

list.title: Monitor your blood glucose:
list.snippet: Learn how to use a glucose meter and/or a continuous glucose monitor (CGM) to track your blood sugar levels.

list.title: Adopt a healthy diet:
list.snippet: Focus on a balanced diet with plenty of fruits, vegetables, lean proteins, and whole grains.

list.title: Incorporate physical activity:
list.snippet: Aim for at least 30 minutes of moderate-intensity exercise most days of the week.

list.title: Manage stress:
list.snippet: Find healthy ways to cope with stress, such as exercise, meditation, or spending time in nature.

list.title: Get enough sleep:
list.snippet: Prioritize restorative sleep, as sleep deprivation can affect insulin sensitivity.
Talk to friends and family: Share your diagnosis and seek their support in managing your condition.
Join a support group: Connect with others living with diabetes to share experiences and learn from each other.
Consider therapy or counseling: If you're struggling with the emotional impact of diabetes, seek professional help.
Healthy eating: Pay attention to portion sizes and carbohydrate intake, and choose foods that are low in saturated and trans fats.
Regular exercise: Find activities you enjoy and make them a part of your daily routine.
Regular check-ups: Attend all scheduled appointments with your healthcare team to monitor your progress and adjust your plan as needed.
Medication adherence: If medications are prescribed, take them as directed by your doctor.

related_questions.question: Can you live a long healthy life with diabetes?
related_questions.snippet: The younger a person who receives a type 2 diabetes diagnosis is, the higher the risk that diabetes-linked complications will shorten their lifespan. However, by adopting effective management strategies, there is a good chance that a person living with type 2 diabetes may live as long as a person without the condition.
